body.title: The Vineyards Above Manarola
body.subtitle: One year in the life of a vertical vineyard

body.quote: My grandfather used to say the vines here don't grow—they climb. Like us, they learned long ago that on these slopes, you go up or you go nowhere.
body.leftContent:
The trenino rattles up the slope at dawn, carrying pruning shears and a thermos of coffee. Lorenzo rides it the way his father did, and his grandfather before that—standing with one hand on the rail, watching Manarola shrink below him as the miniature railway climbs toward the terraces.

These aren't vineyards in the way most people imagine them. No rolling green hills or tidy rows you can walk between. The vines above Manarola cling to narrow terraces held in place by muretti a secco—dry stone walls built centuries ago, stacked without mortar by hands that understood the mountain would take back everything if you didn't hold firm.
body.rightContent:
The work happens on slopes so steep that machines are useless. Everything moves by trenino or by shoulder. Every bottle of wine from these hillsides carries the weight of that impossibility—and the stubborn refusal to accept it.

This is the story of one year in a vertical vineyard, where the seasons don't just change the weather—they change everything about how you move, what you carry, and what you hope for when October comes.

body.markdown: In March, when the morning air still carries a chill off the Ligurian Sea, Lorenzo walks the terraces with his secateurs. Each vine gets examined, touched, considered. The Bosco vines—the backbone of every wine made here—get pruned back hard. You're cutting away what grew last year to make room for what will come. It's an act of faith more than agriculture.

The Albarola and Vermentino vines get similar attention, though they're fussier about it. Cut too much and they sulk all season. Too little and they waste energy on growth that won't matter come harvest. His father taught him to listen to the vines, which sounds romantic until you realize it means paying attention to a thousand small signals—the color of the bark, the spacing of the buds, the way each cane bent under last year's fruit.

By April, the terraces turn pale green. The first leaves uncurl, tender and bright, and you start to believe again that this impossible arrangement—vines clinging to cliffs above the sea—might actually work for another year. The muretti a secco warm in the spring sun, holding heat into the cool evenings, creating microclimates in every walled terrace. It's the reason wine can grow here at all.

June brings the real work. The vines grow with a wildness that surprises people who've never seen them. Shoots reach in every direction, trying to escape the discipline of the terrace. Lorenzo and his crew spend weeks tucking and tying, training the growth along wires, cutting away anything that won't bear fruit.

The trenino makes a dozen trips some days, carrying workers up in the morning and down at dusk. There's no shade up here. The sun reflects off the sea and bounces back from the stone walls. You drink water constantly and still feel wrung out by afternoon. But the grapes are forming now—tiny green clusters that will become wine if everything goes right.

body.alt: Terraced vineyard rows climbing steep hillsides in Cinque Terre wine country
body.caption: The terraces climb at angles that defy conventional viticulture—and create wines that defy convention too. Photo by Jonathan Skule on Unsplash

body.markdown: August is waiting weather. The grapes are ripening but not ready. Too much rain now and they'll swell with water instead of sugar. Too much heat and they'll raisin on the vine. Lorenzo walks the terraces every few days, tasting, watching the color change from green to gold, making his calculations about when to call the harvest.

The vendemmia—the harvest—usually comes in late September or early October. There's a week or two when everyone who can hold pruning shears shows up on the terraces. It's the only way the work gets done. You can't harvest these slopes with machines, so you harvest them with neighbors.

The trenino makes trip after trip, hauling plastic crates filled with grapes down to the cantina. Lorenzo makes the same mental calculation his grandfather made: which grapes become regular wine and which become Sciacchetrà. The sweetest, most perfect clusters get set aside. Everything else goes to the press.

body.quote: I was seven the first time my grandfather let me ride the trenino during vendemmia. He handed me a small crate and told me to fill it carefully—no bruised grapes, no leaves, no stems. I felt like I'd been given the most important job in the world. Twenty-five years later, I still feel that way when October comes and the harvest starts. Some responsibilities you grow into; others you grow around.
body.author: Giulia Rossi

body.markdown: By November, the fermentation is underway and the terraces are turning gold and rust. The vines give their last performance before winter—a show of color that tourists come to photograph but that signals to people like Lorenzo that the year's work is nearly done. The leaves will fall, the canes will go dormant, and in a few months it'll be time to prune again.

December through February, the terraces rest. The trenino still runs—there are always walls to repair, always maintenance that couldn't happen during the growing season—but the urgency is gone. This is when Lorenzo walks the vineyards slowly, noticing things. A section of wall that needs attention before spring. A terrace where the drainage isn't quite right. The shape of a vine that will need heavier pruning in March.

The mistral winds blow cold off the mountains, and fog sometimes fills the valley below, leaving the upper terraces floating above a white sea. On clear days you can see Corsica. The vines sleep, but the work of planning next year has already begun.

Most of the wine from these terraces is white—crisp, mineral, made to drink with the anchovies and seafood that come from the waters below. But the wine people remember, the one that justifies all this impossible labor, is Sciacchetrà.

It's made from the same grapes—Bosco primarily, with Albarola and Vermentino—but only from the best clusters, laid out to dry on reed mats for weeks after harvest. The grapes raisin slowly, concentrating their sugars and flavors. By the time they're pressed, they've lost more than half their weight. What remains becomes a wine that's amber-gold and almost painfully intense—honey and apricot and something that tastes like the stone walls themselves.

Locals don't drink it casually. It's a wine for celebrations, for toasts to people who aren't here anymore, for moments that need to be marked. Lorenzo keeps a few bottles back each year, not to sell but to remember what that harvest was like. Twenty years from now, he'll open one and taste October 2026 again—the heat, the work, the particular alchemy of that season's weather and effort.

body.title: Walk Among the Vines
body.content:
The terraces above Manarola aren't a secret—the trails run right through them—but most visitors walk past without understanding what they're seeing. These aren't decorative walls. They're the infrastructure of an ancient, ongoing negotiation between people and landscape.

Visit in spring and you'll see the bright green hope of new growth. Come in October and you might see the harvest happening, crates of grapes moving down the mountain in the late afternoon light. Winter offers the clearest views and the quietest paths.

But any season, the truth is the same: wine from here tastes like it does because of the impossibility of making it at all. That's not romance. It's just what happens when you refuse to accept that something can't be done.
